title: Holding magnitude type fixed weakens a Ridgecrest size and timing test on days 1 to 30
abstract: We tested whether larger events have more nearby events after them than before them in a fixed USGS Ridgecrest catalog. The sample has 931 events with magnitude at least 2.5 on days 1 to 30 after the 2019 M7.1 event. We used 928 central events with full time windows. The score counts events within 10 minutes and 5 km after each event, minus the count before it. The mean score for magnitude at least 3 exceeds that for magnitude 2.5 to less than 3 by 0.197 events. Shuffling size labels within days and 10 km areas gives a null mean of -0.0067 and a one-sided Monte Carlo p value of 0.0001. Also holding magnitude type fixed raises the null mean to 0.1348 and gives p = 0.0566. The observed score is inside that null model's central 95% range. All 629 small events use local magnitude, while 98 of 299 larger events use other magnitude types. This lack of shared size ranges limits a scale-controlled comparison. The type check does not prove that the scales cause the timing pattern. The result is a catalog diagnostic, not a physical productivity estimate. One sequence, missed events, mixed scales, conditional exchange assumptions, and retrospective data limit inference. The package gives fixed data, code, all null draws, a figure, and an independent audit.

display.caption: The left panel gives the primary shuffle distribution. The right panel gives observed departures from each exact null mean and central 95% null reference ranges. These are not confidence intervals for physical effects. Holding magnitude type fixed weakens the evidence.
